title: Utang na Loob and Financial Decision-Making: A Qualitative Study of Filipino Family Financial Obligations
authors: Donato, M. L.; Santos, A. B.; Reyes, A. C.
tldr: Qualitative study of 30 Filipino families reveals that utang na loob (debt of gratitude) significantly influences financial decision-making, leading to prioritization of extended family obligations over personal financial goals and creating complex interpersonal financial dependencies.
problem_and_motivation: Utang na loob is a core Filipino cultural value involving reciprocal obligations, but its impact on personal financial management and decision-making is poorly understood. Existing PFMS are designed for individualistic contexts and may not accommodate collectivist financial dynamics.
approach: Qualitative study using in-depth interviews with 30 Filipino family financial decision-makers across Metro Manila and provincial areas.
Purposeful sampling: diverse socioeconomic backgrounds, family structures (nuclear, extended, multi-generational).
Interview protocol: semi-structured exploring financial obligations, decision-making processes, family expectations, and the role of utang na loob.
Data analysis: Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) with independent coding by two researchers and consensus discussion.
Member checking and triangulation with family members where possible.
Cross-case analysis by income level, family structure, and geographic location.
findings: Utang na loob creates binding financial obligations that often override personal budget priorities.

Three types of utang na loob financial obligations: immediate family support (education, medical), extended family support (siblings, cousins), and community obligations (fiestas, weddings, funerals).
Extended family support obligations are the most disruptive to personal budgets because they are unpredictable.
Refusing financial requests due to utang na loob leads to social consequences (hiya — shame, loss of face).
Families develop coping strategies: rotating savings (paluwagan), informal IOUs, and multi-party lending arrangements.
Collective budgeting (pooled family income) practice reported by 43% of participants.
PFMS usage is individual-focused; 67% of participants express need for family/shared financial management features.
Financial secrecy (hidden savings, undisclosed debt) exists alongside collective obligations as a coping mechanism.

Filipino concept of shame, loss of social face, or embarrassment.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: Provides critical cultural contextualization for PFMS design in the Philippines. Demonstrates that utang na loob creates financial dynamics (unpredictable obligations, collective budgeting, financial secrecy) that existing PFMS do not accommodate. The finding that 67% of participants desire shared/family financial management features is a direct design implication for PFMS targeting Filipino users.
directly_justifies: Utang na loob obligations override personal budget priorities.
Extended family obligations are unpredictable and most disruptive to budgets.
67% of participants express need for shared/family financial management features.
Collective budgeting (pooled income) is practiced by 43% of participants.
Financial secrecy coexists with collective obligations as a coping mechanism.
limits: Focus on one cultural mechanism; other cultural factors not explored. [unacknowledged]
Self-reported obligations may not match actual financial flows. [unacknowledged]
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all 14 topic domains was performed. Domains 2.A (cultural nuances) and 13.B (debt management) were flagged as highly relevant because utang na loob is a cultural mechanism creating informal financial obligations. Domain 2.C was flagged as medium relevance for informal financial arrangements. Domain 3.A was flagged as low relevance for spending obligations. Domains 1, 4-12, 14 were rejected as the study is a qualitative cultural analysis without connection to young professionals, ML, or system design.
